claims.text: The starting material is as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high mechanical strength at room temperature and elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C.
The proposed intervention is partial replacement of Hf with additional Ti while holding the other alloy components fixed.
Partial replacement of Hf with Ti will decrease the density of HfMoTaTiZr.
Partial replacement of Hf with Ti will preserve yield strength and ductility at room temperature and near 1000 °C.
The Hf-to-Ti substitution will retain a single-phase BCC solid solution.
Lattice distortion will be preserved after Hf is partially replaced by Ti.
Solid-solution strengthening will be preserved after Hf is partially replaced by Ti.
Replacing heavy Hf with lighter Ti reduces average atomic weight and thereby reduces alloy density.
Increasing Ti supports solid-solution strengthening and phase stability.
Ti and Zr additions can produce lower-density alloys while contributing to elevated-temperature strength.
The modified alloy may achieve a density reduction of approximately 5–10%.
The proposed result applies to as-cast microstructures tested from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C under comparable loading regimes.
The optimal amount of Hf replacement by Ti is not known and requires experimental calibration.
Candidate substitution levels of 10%, 20%, and 30% can be compared using density, XRD, and room-temperature and 1000 °C mechanical tests.
The hypothesis is rejected if a substituted alloy lowers density by less than approximately 5% or loses more than 10–15% of yield strength or ductility at either test temperature.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis promises preservation of strength and ductility with little to no degradation, but the rejection rule would permit losses as large as 10–15% without falsification.
The optimal substitution level is stated to be unknown, yet failure of any one candidate composition is said to falsify the entire hypothesis, even if another substitution level succeeds.
